welcome_lead: Today's adventure: D2.1 Cell and nuclear division — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic D2.1.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering D2.1 Cell and nuclear division, guide topic D2.1.
final_note: You worked through D2.1 Cell and nuclear division — 17 guide statements.

concepts.def: The process by which a parent cell (often called a mother cell) divides to produce two daughter cells. In all living organisms new cells are generated only in this way: the parent cell does not persist alongside its daughters, and its entire contents, including the divided nucleus in eukaryotes, are shared out between the two daughter cells.

One of the two cells produced when a parent cell divides. Each division produces exactly two daughter cells; the very large numbers of cells in a multicellular organism arise from many repeated rounds of division, not from one cell splitting into many.

The splitting of the cytoplasm of a parent cell between the two daughter cells. It follows nuclear division and is not itself a phase of mitosis. In an animal cell a ring of contractile actin and myosin proteins pinches the cell membrane together from the outside inwards; in a plant cell vesicles gather at the equator and fuse to assemble sections of new membrane and cell wall from the inside outwards.

A ring of actin and myosin protein filaments that forms just inside the cell membrane at the equator of a dividing animal cell. The ring contracts, using the same actin–myosin interaction as a muscle, so the membrane is pulled inwards as a cleavage furrow until the cytoplasm is pinched into two.

The structure that divides a plant cell during cytokinesis. Vesicles carrying membrane and cell wall material are moved to the equator of the cell, where they fuse into a growing disc of new membrane enclosing new cell wall; the disc expands outwards until it joins the existing cell wall, separating the two daughter cells.

Division of the cytoplasm of a parent cell into two daughter cells of unequal size. Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not in every case. Whether it is equal or not, both daughter cells must receive at least one mitochondrion, and at least one of any other organelle that can only be made by dividing a pre-existing structure, such as a chloroplast, because such organelles cannot be assembled from scratch.

The production of egg cells in humans, an example of unequal cytokinesis. In each of the two meiotic divisions the cytoplasm is divided very unequally: the future egg cell keeps almost all of the cytoplasm and organelles, while a very small polar body receives a full set of chromosomes but almost no cytoplasm and degenerates. The chromosomes are shared equally; only the cytoplasm is divided unequally.

Asexual reproduction of yeast by unequal cytokinesis. A small bud grows out from the parent cell; the nucleus divides by mitosis and one of the two nuclei moves into the bud, together with a share of the organelles including mitochondria. The bud is then separated from the much larger parent cell and grows to full size.

Nuclear division in eukaryotes that produces two nuclei with the same chromosome number and the same genome as the parent nucleus, so the daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent. Mitosis is used for growth, cell replacement, tissue repair and asexual reproduction. Nuclear division must precede cell division; otherwise daughter cells without a nucleus (anucleate cells) would be produced.

Nuclear division in eukaryotes that halves the chromosome number, producing four haploid nuclei from one diploid nucleus in two successive divisions, and that generates genetic diversity among the nuclei produced. In a sexual life cycle it produces haploid cells (gametes, or in plants spores that give rise to gamete-producing cells), so that fusion of gametes at fertilization restores the diploid number.

A cell that has no nucleus. If the cytoplasm of a cell were divided without the nucleus first dividing, one of the daughter cells would be anucleate, with no chromosomes and so no genes to transcribe; nuclear division before cell division avoids this.

The two identical, elongated DNA molecules that make up one chromosome after DNA replication. Each chromatid is an exact copy of the other, produced by DNA replication during interphase, and the two are held together at the centromere until anaphase (anaphase II in meiosis), when they separate and each becomes a chromosome in its own right.

concepts.term: DNA replication as a prerequisite for nuclear division
concepts.def: The copying of every DNA molecule in the nucleus during interphase, before either mitosis or meiosis begins. Replication doubles the amount of DNA without changing the chromosome number: each chromosome comes to consist of two chromatids. Before meiosis, DNA is replicated once only; there is no replication between meiosis I and meiosis II.

One of a group of basic proteins around which DNA is wound in eukaryotic chromosomes. The DNA–histone complexes (nucleosomes) are packed together and the resulting fibre is coiled and supercoiled, condensing the very long DNA molecule into a chromosome short and thick enough to be moved without tangling or breaking.

The supercoiling of DNA around histones that makes chromosomes shorter and thicker at the start of both mitosis and meiosis. During interphase the DNA is extended so that it can be transcribed and replicated; condensation occurs only for nuclear division, after which the chromosomes decondense again.

Protein tubes that grow from the poles of a dividing cell and attach to the centromeres of chromosomes. Together with microtubule motor proteins they move chromosomes: to the equator before they are separated and towards the poles during anaphase. Microtubules do not contract; they lengthen and shorten by adding or removing subunits at their ends.

A protein that binds to a microtubule and uses energy from ATP to move along it. Motor proteins at the centromere of a chromosome move the chromosome along spindle microtubules, and shortening of the microtubules accompanies this movement towards the pole. Chromosome movement in mitosis and meiosis depends on microtubules and microtubule motors.
The first phase of mitosis. Chromosomes condense by supercoiling and become visible as two chromatids joined at the centromere, the nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle begins to form.

The second phase of mitosis. Spindle microtubules attached to the centromeres move the chromosomes so that they line up on a single plane at the equator of the cell, with the two chromatids of each chromosome facing opposite poles.

The third phase of mitosis. The centromeres divide, the sister chromatids of each chromosome are separated and moved to opposite poles by microtubules and motor proteins, and each chromatid is now a chromosome. Because the two chromatids were identical, each pole receives an identical set.

The final phase of mitosis. The chromosomes reach the poles, a nuclear envelope forms around each set and the chromosomes decondense. Two genetically identical nuclei now exist; cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm between them.

Recognizing the phase of a cell in a diagram, in a micrograph or under a microscope from the state of its chromosomes and nuclear envelope: an intact nucleus with no distinct chromosomes is interphase (not a phase of mitosis); condensed chromosomes visible but scattered through the cell, not aligned on one plane, is prophase (the nuclear envelope breaks down during this phase); chromosomes aligned on one plane across the equator is metaphase; two separated sets of chromatids moving apart is anaphase; two groups at the poles with nuclear envelopes re-forming is telophase.

Describes a nucleus or cell with two complete sets of chromosomes, one set inherited from each parent, so that every chromosome has a homologous partner. The diploid number is written 2n; in humans 2n = 46.

Describes a nucleus or cell with one complete set of chromosomes, one of each type. A haploid cell has one copy of every gene, not half of the genes. The haploid number is written n; in humans n = 23. Gametes are haploid.

A description of meiosis, which halves the chromosome number. One diploid nucleus undergoes two divisions to produce four haploid nuclei. Meiosis I separates the two chromosomes of each homologous pair (the reduction); meiosis II separates the sister chromatids of each chromosome. The DNA is replicated once, before meiosis I, and not again between the two divisions.

The two chromosomes of a pair in a diploid cell, one from each parent, that carry the same genes in the same sequence but may carry different alleles of those genes. Homologous chromosomes are separate chromosomes; they are not the two chromatids of one replicated chromosome.

concepts.term: Need for meiosis in a sexual life cycle
concepts.def: Fertilization fuses the nuclei of two gametes, adding their chromosomes together. If gametes were not haploid the chromosome number would double in every generation. Meiosis halves the number when gametes are produced, so fertilization restores the diploid number and it stays constant from one generation to the next.

The failure of a pair of homologous chromosomes to separate in anaphase I, or of sister chromatids to separate in anaphase II, of meiosis. Both members go to the same pole, so one gamete produced has an extra chromosome and another lacks that chromosome.

The condition that results when non-disjunction of chromosome 21 in meiosis produces a gamete with two copies of chromosome 21; fertilization by a normal gamete gives a zygote with three copies (trisomy 21) and 47 chromosomes in its cells. It is an error in chromosome number arising in meiosis, not a change in the base sequence of a gene.

A pair of homologous chromosomes lying side by side during prophase I and metaphase I of meiosis, each chromosome consisting of two chromatids. Crossing over takes place between non-sister chromatids of a bivalent, and bivalents are oriented randomly on the equator at metaphase I.

At metaphase I each bivalent lines up on the equator with its maternal and paternal chromosomes facing either pole at random, independently of every other bivalent. Each gamete still receives exactly one chromosome of each pair, but which one is a matter of chance, so a cell with n pairs can produce 2ⁿ different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes (2²³, about 8 million, in humans).

The exchange of lengths of DNA between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes while they are paired as a bivalent in prophase I. It produces chromatids with new combinations of the alleles already present on the two homologues; it does not create new alleles.

Increase in the number of cells by repeated rounds of the cell cycle. It brings about growth (in plant meristems and in early-stage animal embryos), routine replacement of cells lost from tissues such as skin, and repair of tissues, for example during the healing of a skin wound.

A region of a plant, such as the tip of a root or shoot, in which cells proliferate by mitosis and cytokinesis. Cell division for growth in plants is confined to meristems; cells elsewhere grow by enlargement and differentiate but do not usually divide.

The sequence of events by which a cell proliferates: interphase, consisting of G1, S and G2 in that order, followed by mitosis and then cytokinesis. The daughter cells then enter G1 of the next cycle. Interphase occupies most of the cycle; mitosis is a relatively short part of it.

The three stages of interphase. In G1 the cell grows, synthesizing proteins and other components and increasing its organelles; in S phase the DNA is replicated so that each chromosome comes to consist of two chromatids; in G2 the cell continues to grow and prepares for mitosis. DNA replication occurs only in S phase.

Interphase is a metabolically active period, not a resting one. The cell grows by biosynthesis of its components, including proteins (throughout interphase) and DNA (in S phase). Mitochondria, and chloroplasts in plant cells, increase in number by growth and division of the existing organelles, so that the daughter cells will each receive them.

One of a group of proteins whose concentrations rise and fall during the cell cycle and that control progress through it. Different cyclins rise and fall at different points in the cycle; the concentration of a specific cyclin must reach a threshold level for the cell to pass a particular checkpoint, after which its concentration falls again.

A point in the cell cycle at which progress to the next stage is controlled. The cell passes a checkpoint only when a threshold concentration of a specific cyclin has been reached, so the cycle cannot proceed until the necessary preparation is complete.

A proto-oncogene is a normal gene present in every cell whose product stimulates progress through the cell cycle. A mutation can convert it into an oncogene, whose product is over-active or produced in excess, so that the cell is driven to divide without the normal controls.

A normal gene whose product restrains the cell cycle, for example by halting it at a checkpoint when DNA is damaged. Mutations that stop a tumour suppressor gene from working remove this restraint. Mutations in tumour suppressor genes and in proto-oncogenes both result in uncontrolled cell division and the formation of a tumour.

A mass of cells formed by uncontrolled cell division. Tumours differ in their rates of cell division and growth and in whether they invade neighbouring tissue and spread. A benign tumour does not cause cancer; a malignant tumour does.

A tumour whose cells remain together in one place, do not invade neighbouring tissue and do not spread to other parts of the body. A benign tumour is still the product of uncontrolled division and may cause harm by pressing on surrounding structures, but it does not cause cancer.

A tumour whose cells invade neighbouring tissue and can detach, travel in the blood or lymph and establish tumours elsewhere. Malignant tumours cause cancer; they are distinguished from benign tumours by invasion and the capacity for metastasis, not by their size or rate of growth alone.

A primary tumour is the tumour at the site where uncontrolled division began. Metastasis is the movement of cells from a malignant primary tumour to other parts of the body, where they form secondary tumours of the same cell type as the primary.

The proportion of cells in a population that are in mitosis: the number of cells with visible condensed chromosomes in any phase of mitosis divided by the total number of cells observed, expressed as a fraction or a percentage. A high mitotic index indicates rapid proliferation, whether in a tumour or in a normal tissue such as a meristem.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes how new cells are generated in a living organism?
options: A parent cell divides to produce two daughter cells, and everything the parent contained is shared out between them.
A parent cell produces two daughter cells and then goes on living alongside them as a third cell.
A parent cell splits at one moment into many small daughter cells, which then grow to full size in the tissue.
A parent cell splits its cytoplasm into two halves, each of which then assembles a nucleus of its own from the cytoplasm.
mcqs.specStatementText: New cells only come from cells dividing
mcqs.explain: In all living organisms new cells arise by division of a parent (mother) cell into two daughter cells. The parent cell does not persist; its whole contents are divided between the two daughters.
rationales: In all living organisms new cells arise by division of a parent (mother) cell into two daughter cells. The parent cell does not persist; its whole contents are divided between the two daughters.
A student who reads 'mother' and 'daughter' as a human family picks this. The parent cell is the material from which the two daughter cells are made; no third cell remains.
A student who pictures one cell fragmenting into many picks this. Each division produces exactly two daughter cells; large numbers come from repeated divisions.
A student who thinks a nucleus can be built from scratch picks this. The nucleus divides first by mitosis or meiosis, and each daughter cell receives one of the two nuclei produced.

mcqs.q: How does cytokinesis in an animal cell differ from cytokinesis in a plant cell?
options: Both cells are pinched in two by a contractile ring, but in a plant cell the ring acts more slowly because it must squeeze the wall as well.
An animal cell is pinched in two by a ring of actin and myosin; a plant cell builds new membrane and wall from vesicles at its equator.
An animal cell is pinched in two by spindle microtubules; a plant cell builds new membrane and wall from vesicles at its equator.
An animal cell is pinched in two by a ring of actin and myosin; in a plant cell the existing wall grows inwards from the edges until it meets.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm, differently in animals and plants
mcqs.explain: In an animal cell a ring of contractile actin and myosin proteins pinches the cell membrane together. In a plant cell vesicles assemble sections of membrane and cell wall at the equator, which grow outwards to divide the cell.
rationales: A student who applies the GCSE 'the cytoplasm divides' model to every cell picks this. A plant cell cannot be pinched through its rigid wall; a cell plate is built from vesicles instead.

In an animal cell a ring of contractile actin and myosin proteins pinches the cell membrane together. In a plant cell vesicles assemble sections of membrane and cell wall at the equator, which grow outwards to divide the cell.
A student who merges the spindle with the contractile ring picks this. Microtubules move chromosomes; the ring that pinches an animal cell is made of actin and myosin.
A student who makes the old wall do the furrowing picks this. The new wall in a plant cell starts at the centre, as a cell plate formed from vesicles, and grows outwards to join the existing wall.

mcqs.q: A dividing cell is examined after its two new nuclei have formed. Many small vesicles are seen gathering and fusing in a line across the equator of the cell, midway between the nuclei. Which conclusion is justified?
options: It is a plant cell: the vesicles mark the line along which the cell membrane will be pinched inwards to split the cytoplasm.
It is a plant cell: the vesicles carry enzymes that soften the existing wall so that it can grow inwards across the cell.
It is a plant cell: the vesicles are assembling sections of new membrane and cell wall to separate the daughter cells.
It is an animal cell: the vesicles are new organelles that have been made from scratch so that each daughter cell has a full set.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm, differently in animals and plants
mcqs.explain: Vesicles fusing at the equator to form a cell plate is the mechanism of cytokinesis in plant cells. The fused vesicle membranes become the new cell membranes and their contents become the new cell wall.
rationales: A student who expects every cell to pinch in two picks this. Pinching by a contractile ring is the animal mechanism; a plant cell is divided by a cell plate built from the vesicles themselves.
A student who thinks the old wall closes like a furrow picks this. The existing wall takes no active part; the vesicles at the equator build a completely new wall that grows outwards.

Vesicles fusing at the equator to form a cell plate is the mechanism of cytokinesis in plant cells. The fused vesicle membranes become the new cell membranes and their contents become the new cell wall.

A student who thinks organelles are assembled from raw materials at division picks this. Organelles such as mitochondria are made by division of existing ones, and vesicles fusing at the equator identify a plant cell forming a cell plate.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the division of the cytoplasm between two daughter cells is correct?
options: The cytoplasm is divided equally in every cell division, so that each daughter cell receives exactly half of each type of organelle.
A daughter cell that receives no mitochondria can synthesize new ones from proteins made on its ribosomes, so none need be shared.
When cytoplasm is divided unequally, the daughter cell that receives more cytoplasm also receives the larger share of the chromosomes.
Each daughter cell must receive at least one mitochondrion, because mitochondria form only by division of existing ones.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not always
mcqs.explain: Mitochondria, like chloroplasts, can only be made by division of a pre-existing organelle. A daughter cell that received none could not make any, so at least one must be passed to each cell.
rationales: A student who has only seen symmetrical diagrams picks this. Division of the cytoplasm is usually equal but not in all cases; oogenesis and yeast budding are unequal.
A student who thinks a cell can build any structure from raw materials picks this. Mitochondria arise only from existing mitochondria, which is exactly why each daughter must receive at least one.
A student who equates the size of a cell with its share of everything picks this. The chromosomes are shared equally by nuclear division; only the cytoplasm is divided unequally.
Mitochondria, like chloroplasts, can only be made by division of a pre-existing organelle. A daughter cell that received none could not make any, so at least one must be passed to each cell.

mcqs.q: In human oogenesis, the first meiotic division produces a large secondary oocyte and a very small polar body. What does this unequal cytokinesis achieve?
options: The oocyte keeps almost all the cytoplasm and organelles for the future zygote, while both cells receive a complete haploid set of chromosomes.
The oocyte receives a larger share of the chromosomes along with the extra cytoplasm, so the polar body has fewer chromosomes to be discarded.
The polar body is the result of a failed equal division; in normal oogenesis the cytoplasm is divided equally between two egg cells of equal size.
The polar body is a fragment of cytoplasm pinched off without a nucleus, so the oocyte keeps all of the chromosomes from the division.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not always
mcqs.explain: Unequal cytokinesis concentrates the cytoplasm, with its organelles and nutrient stores, in the one cell that can become an egg. Nuclear division has already shared the chromosomes equally, so the polar body has a full haploid set but almost no cytoplasm.
rationales: Unequal cytokinesis concentrates the cytoplasm, with its organelles and nutrient stores, in the one cell that can become an egg. Nuclear division has already shared the chromosomes equally, so the polar body has a full haploid set but almost no cytoplasm.
A student who thinks a bigger cell must hold more genetic material picks this. Meiosis I gives each product one chromosome of every pair; the inequality is only in the cytoplasm.
A student who believes cytokinesis is invariably equal picks this. Unequal division is the normal course of human oogenesis and is one of the guide's two examples of unequal cytokinesis.

A student who pictures a bud or fragment forming without nuclear division picks this. The polar body receives one of the two nuclei produced by meiosis I; it is small because it receives almost no cytoplasm.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly compares the roles of mitosis and meiosis in eukaryotes?
options: Mitosis keeps the full set of genes in each cell, whereas meiosis produces cells that carry only half of the organism's genes.
Mitosis keeps the chromosome number and genome of the cell the same, whereas meiosis halves the chromosome number and generates diversity.
Mitosis doubles the chromosome number, which meiosis then halves, so together the two processes keep the number constant.
Mitosis separates the two chromosomes of each homologous pair into different cells, whereas meiosis separates the sister chromatids.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mitosis keeps the genome; meiosis halves it and adds variety
mcqs.explain: Mitosis maintains the chromosome number and genome of cells, producing genetically identical nuclei. Meiosis halves the chromosome number and generates genetic diversity among the nuclei it produces.
rationales: A student who hears 'halves the chromosome number' as 'halves the genes' picks this. A haploid nucleus has one chromosome of every pair and so one copy of every gene.
Mitosis maintains the chromosome number and genome of cells, producing genetically identical nuclei. Meiosis halves the chromosome number and generates genetic diversity among the nuclei it produces.
A student who thinks replication or mitosis doubles the chromosome number picks this. Mitosis maintains the number; it is fertilization that doubles it and meiosis that halves it.
A student who transfers the separation of homologues from meiosis to mitosis picks this. Mitosis separates sister chromatids, so both members of every pair go to each daughter cell.

mcqs.q: Nuclear division normally occurs before the cytoplasm of a cell is divided. What would result if a cell divided its cytoplasm into two without first dividing its nucleus?
options: Each daughter cell would build itself a new nucleus from the DNA and proteins present in its share of the cytoplasm.
Both daughter cells would receive a nucleus, because DNA replication has already doubled the number of chromosomes to provide two sets.
One daughter cell would be anucleate: with no chromosomes it could not transcribe genes to replace its proteins or divide again.
This could not happen, because splitting the cytoplasm is the final phase of mitosis and so must follow the division of the nucleus.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mitosis keeps the genome; meiosis halves it and adds variety
mcqs.explain: Nuclear division is needed before cell division to avoid the production of anucleate cells. A cell without a nucleus has no genome, so it can make no new mRNA and cannot divide.
rationales: A student who thinks a nucleus can be assembled like any other organelle picks this. Chromosomes exist only as copies of previous chromosomes, so a nucleus can arise only by division of an existing nucleus.

A student who thinks replication produces two sets of separate chromosomes picks this. Replication produces two chromatids in each chromosome inside one nucleus; only nuclear division can separate them into two nuclei.
Nuclear division is needed before cell division to avoid the production of anucleate cells. A cell without a nucleus has no genome, so it can make no new mRNA and cannot divide.
A student who treats cytokinesis as a phase of mitosis picks this. Cytokinesis is a separate process from nuclear division, which is why the guide emphasizes that nuclear division is needed first.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of a chromosome after DNA replication and before anaphase?
options: Two DNA molecules, one inherited from each parent, joined together to form a homologous pair.
A single elongated DNA molecule, which is not copied to form a second chromatid until prophase.
Two separate chromosomes, each with one DNA molecule, so that the chromosome number has doubled.
Two identical elongated DNA molecules, the sister chromatids, held together at the centromere.
mcqs.specStatementText: DNA is replicated once before either division
mcqs.explain: After replication each chromosome consists of two elongated DNA molecules (chromatids), exact copies of each other, which remain held together until anaphase.
rationales: A student who reads the X-shaped diagram as a homologous pair picks this. The two chromatids are identical copies made by replication; homologous chromosomes are separate chromosomes.
A student who thinks the second chromatid appears when chromosomes condense picks this. Replication is complete in interphase; prophase only makes the two existing chromatids visible.
A student who counts each chromatid as a chromosome picks this. Until anaphase the two chromatids are held together and count as one chromosome, so the chromosome number is unchanged.
After replication each chromosome consists of two elongated DNA molecules (chromatids), exact copies of each other, which remain held together until anaphase.

mcqs.q: A cell of an organism has 8 chromosomes before its DNA is replicated. How many chromosomes and how many DNA molecules are in its nucleus at metaphase of mitosis?
options: 8 chromosomes, 16 DNA molecules
16 chromosomes, 16 DNA molecules
8 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules
16 chromosomes, 32 molecules of DNA
mcqs.specStatementText: DNA is replicated once before either division
mcqs.explain: Replication before mitosis gives each of the 8 chromosomes two chromatids, each a DNA molecule, so there are 16 DNA molecules. The chromatids stay joined until anaphase, so the chromosome number is still 8.
rationales: Replication before mitosis gives each of the 8 chromosomes two chromatids, each a DNA molecule, so there are 16 DNA molecules. The chromatids stay joined until anaphase, so the chromosome number is still 8.
A student who counts each chromatid as a chromosome picks this. Two chromatids held together at the centromere are one chromosome; the number does not double until anaphase separates them.

A student who thinks replication has not yet happened at metaphase picks this. DNA replication is a prerequisite for mitosis and is complete in interphase, so each chromosome already has two chromatids.
A student who doubles the chromosome number at replication and then gives each 'new' chromosome two chromatids picks this. Replication doubles the DNA once; the chromosome number stays at 8.

mcqs.q: How is the DNA of a eukaryotic chromosome condensed before nuclear division?
options: The double helix itself twists ever more tightly, with no proteins involved, until the molecule is short enough to be seen.
The DNA is wound around histone proteins, and the fibre so formed is supercoiled into a much shorter, thicker structure.
The DNA is already packed as a condensed chromosome throughout the cycle; staining at division merely makes it visible.
The DNA is copied, and the two new copies pack tightly against each other to form the short, visible chromosome.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chromosomes condense and are moved by microtubules in both divisions
mcqs.explain: Condensation depends on histones: DNA wound around histones forms nucleosomes, and the DNA–protein fibre is then coiled and supercoiled, shortening the chromosome so it can be moved without tangling.
rationales: A student who hears 'supercoiling' as more of the helix's own coiling picks this. The naked helix cannot be packed into a chromosome; the coiling is of DNA wound around histone proteins.
Condensation depends on histones: DNA wound around histones forms nucleosomes, and the DNA–protein fibre is then coiled and supercoiled, shortening the chromosome so it can be moved without tangling.
A student who takes the karyotype image as the permanent state of DNA picks this. Between divisions the DNA is extended for transcription and replication; it condenses only for nuclear division.
A student who confuses replication with condensation picks this. Replication happens in interphase and produces two chromatids; it is supercoiling around histones, not copying, that shortens them.

mcqs.q: In both mitosis and meiosis, chromosomes are moved to the poles of the cell during anaphase. What causes this movement?
options: The spindle microtubules contract in the same way as muscle fibres, pulling the chromosomes towards the poles.
The separated chromatids repel one another and so drift apart to opposite ends of the cell without any attachment.
Microtubule motor proteins move the chromosomes along spindle microtubules, which shorten as the chromosomes travel.
A ring of actin and myosin at each pole contracts, dragging the chromosomes attached to it away from the equator.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chromosomes condense and are moved by microtubules in both divisions
mcqs.explain: Chromosome movement uses microtubules and microtubule motors. Motor proteins at the centromere move the chromosome along the microtubule towards the pole, and the microtubule shortens as it does so.
rationales: A student who takes 'the fibres pull' literally picks this. Microtubules cannot contract; they shorten by losing subunits, and the movement is produced by motor proteins.
A student who has seen anaphase drawn without a spindle picks this. Chromatids do not move on their own; each is attached at its centromere to microtubules and moved by motor proteins.
Chromosome movement uses microtubules and microtubule motors. Motor proteins at the centromere move the chromosome along the microtubule towards the pole, and the microtubule shortens as it does so.

A student who merges the contractile ring with the spindle picks this. Actin and myosin form the ring that pinches an animal cell in cytokinesis; chromosomes are moved by microtubules and their motors.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the phases of mitosis in a human cell is correct?
options: In anaphase, the two chromosomes of each homologous pair are separated and moved to opposite poles.
In metaphase, the chromosomes line up at the equator while still enclosed within the nuclear envelope.
In prophase, each chromosome is replicated so that it consists of two chromatids by the end of the phase.
In anaphase, the sister chromatids of each chromosome are separated and moved to opposite poles.
mcqs.specStatementText: The four phases of mitosis
mcqs.explain: Anaphase is the phase in which the centromeres divide and the two identical chromatids of every chromosome are moved to opposite poles, so that each pole receives a complete, identical set.
rationales: A student who transfers the separation of homologues from meiosis I to mitosis picks this. Mitosis separates chromatids, keeping both homologues of every pair in each daughter nucleus.
A student who thinks the nuclear envelope persists picks this. The envelope breaks down in prophase so that spindle microtubules can attach to the chromosomes; it re-forms in telophase.
A student who thinks chromatids are made when chromosomes appear picks this. Replication takes place in interphase; in prophase the two existing chromatids become visible as the chromosome condenses.
Anaphase is the phase in which the centromeres divide and the two identical chromatids of every chromosome are moved to opposite poles, so that each pole receives a complete, identical set.

mcqs.q: A parent cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. Why are the two daughter cells genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell?
options: Every chromosome was replicated into two identical chromatids before division, and one chromatid of every chromosome goes to each daughter cell.
Each daughter cell receives half of the parent cell's 46 chromosomes and then replicates them to restore the full set of 46.
Each daughter cell receives one chromosome from each of the 23 homologous pairs, and both chromosomes of a pair carry the same genes.
Mitosis first doubles the number of chromosomes to 92, and then 46 of them are moved into each of the two daughter cells.
mcqs.specStatementText: The four phases of mitosis
mcqs.explain: Replication makes an exact copy of each chromosome as its sister chromatid. Anaphase sends one chromatid of every chromosome to each pole, so both daughter nuclei receive 46 chromosomes carrying the same genome as the parent.
rationales: Replication makes an exact copy of each chromosome as its sister chromatid. Anaphase sends one chromatid of every chromosome to each pole, so both daughter nuclei receive 46 chromosomes carrying the same genome as the parent.

A student who thinks division halves the genetic material picks this. Each daughter cell receives all 46 chromosomes, one chromatid of each; replicating 23 chromosomes could not recreate the other 23.

A student who applies meiosis I to mitosis picks this. Homologues carry the same genes but may carry different alleles, so cells receiving different homologues would not be identical; mitosis gives each daughter both homologues of every pair.

A student who counts chromatids as chromosomes picks this. Replication doubles the DNA, not the chromosome number; there are 46 chromosomes of two chromatids each, until anaphase separates the chromatids.

mcqs.q: Two cells are seen in a stained micrograph of a root tip. Cell 1 has an intact nucleus in which no separate chromosomes can be distinguished. Cell 2 has no nuclear envelope, and its condensed chromosomes lie in a single line across the middle of the cell. Which identification is correct?
options: Cell 1 is in prophase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in prophase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in early anaphase.
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading the phase from a diagram or micrograph
mcqs.explain: An intact nucleus with no distinct chromosomes shows a cell between divisions, in interphase. Condensed chromosomes aligned on one plane at the equator, with the nuclear envelope gone, define metaphase.
rationales: A student who counts interphase as the first stage of mitosis picks this. Prophase is recognized by condensed, visible chromosomes; a cell with an intact nucleus and no distinct chromosomes is in interphase.

An intact nucleus with no distinct chromosomes shows a cell between divisions, in interphase. Condensed chromosomes aligned on one plane at the equator, with the nuclear envelope gone, define metaphase.

A student who identifies prophase by 'condensed but not yet separating' picks this. Chromosomes aligned in a single plane at the equator are the defining feature of metaphase; in prophase they are scattered.

A student who has swapped the names of the two middle phases picks this. Anaphase begins when the chromatids separate and move apart; while the chromosomes are still aligned on the equator the cell is in metaphase.

mcqs.q: A student counted 100 cells in a micrograph of a growing root tip. 85 cells had an intact nucleus with no visible chromosomes; 6 had condensed chromosomes scattered through the cell; 3 had chromosomes aligned across the equator; 4 had two groups of chromatids moving apart; 2 had two groups of chromosomes at the poles with nuclear envelopes forming. Which conclusion is correct?
options: All 100 cells are in mitosis, because the 85 with an intact nucleus and no visible chromosomes are in prophase.
Nine of the cells are in metaphase, because scattered and aligned condensed chromosomes both lie in the middle of the cell.
About 15% of the cells are in mitosis, and prophase is the most frequent phase among the dividing cells.
The tissue has stopped dividing, because far fewer than half of the cells show any phase of mitosis.
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading the phase from a diagram or micrograph
mcqs.explain: The 85 cells with an intact nucleus are in interphase. The other 15 are in mitosis: 6 prophase, 3 metaphase, 4 anaphase and 2 telophase, so 15% of the cells are dividing and prophase is the commonest phase.
rationales: A student who takes interphase to be a stage of mitosis picks this. An intact nucleus with no distinct chromosomes is the appearance of interphase; only the 15 cells with condensed chromosomes are in mitosis.

A student who identifies metaphase by position rather than alignment picks this. Only the 3 cells with chromosomes aligned across the equator are in metaphase; the 6 with scattered chromosomes are in prophase.

The 85 cells with an intact nucleus are in interphase. The other 15 are in mitosis: 6 prophase, 3 metaphase, 4 anaphase and 2 telophase, so 15% of the cells are dividing and prophase is the commonest phase.
A student who expects mitosis to occupy most of the cycle picks this. Interphase is much the longest part of the cell cycle, so 15% of cells in mitosis is typical of an actively growing root tip.

mcqs.q: A diploid nucleus of an organism with 2n = 14 undergoes meiosis. What is produced?
options: Four diploid nuclei, each containing 14 chromosomes
Four haploid nuclei, each with half of the organism's genes
Two haploid nuclei, each containing 7 chromosomes
Four haploid nuclei, each containing 7 chromosomes
mcqs.specStatementText: Meiosis: two divisions, one diploid nucleus to four haploid
mcqs.explain: Meiosis is a reduction division: two successive divisions produce four haploid nuclei from one diploid nucleus. With 2n = 14, each haploid nucleus has n = 7 chromosomes, one of each homologous pair.
rationales: A student who thinks the DNA is replicated again between the two divisions picks this. There is one replication before meiosis I only, so the two divisions halve the chromosome number.
A student who equates half the chromosomes with half the genes picks this. Each haploid nucleus has one chromosome of every pair and therefore one copy of every gene.
A student who thinks meiosis is a single halving division picks this. Meiosis I produces two nuclei and meiosis II divides each again, giving four haploid nuclei.
Meiosis is a reduction division: two successive divisions produce four haploid nuclei from one diploid nucleus. With 2n = 14, each haploid nucleus has n = 7 chromosomes, one of each homologous pair.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly outlines the two rounds of segregation in meiosis?
options: In meiosis I the two chromosomes of each homologous pair separate; in meiosis II the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate.
In meiosis I the sister chromatids of each chromosome are separated, and in meiosis II the homologous chromosomes of each pair are separated.
In meiosis I the homologous chromosomes are separated; the DNA is then replicated so that meiosis II can separate the new chromatids.
In meiosis I each chromosome is split into its maternal chromatid and its paternal chromatid, and meiosis II shares these between nuclei.
mcqs.specStatementText: Meiosis: two divisions, one diploid nucleus to four haploid
mcqs.explain: Meiosis I is the reduction division: the two chromosomes of each bivalent go to opposite poles, so each nucleus has one chromosome of every pair. Meiosis II separates the two chromatids of each of those chromosomes.
rationales: Meiosis I is the reduction division: the two chromosomes of each bivalent go to opposite poles, so each nucleus has one chromosome of every pair. Meiosis II separates the two chromatids of each of those chromosomes.
A student who assumes the first division is 'the same as mitosis' picks this. The order is the reverse: homologues separate first, chromatids second.
A student who applies 'replicate then divide' to each division picks this. No replication occurs between the divisions; the chromatids separated in meiosis II were made before meiosis I.
A student who thinks the two chromatids come from the two parents picks this. Sister chromatids are identical copies; the maternal and paternal chromosomes are the two members of a homologous pair.

mcqs.q: Why is meiosis needed in a sexual life cycle?
options: Gametes could be produced by mitosis instead, because when two diploid gametes fuse the zygote they form is diploid like its parents.
Fertilization combines the chromosomes of two gametes, so the number must be halved beforehand to keep it constant across generations.
Each gamete must carry only half of the parent's genes, so that the offspring gets one half from each parent and no gene is duplicated.
Mitosis doubles the chromosome number each time a body cell divides, so meiosis is needed to bring the number back down again.
mcqs.specStatementText: Meiosis: two divisions, one diploid nucleus to four haploid
mcqs.explain: Fusion of two gametes adds their chromosome sets together. Halving the number in meiosis means that fertilization restores the diploid number instead of doubling it, so the number stays constant from one generation to the next.
rationales: A student who does not track the chromosomes through fertilization picks this. Two diploid gametes would give a zygote with four sets, and the number would double in every generation.

Fusion of two gametes adds their chromosome sets together. Halving the number in meiosis means that fertilization restores the diploid number instead of doubling it, so the number stays constant from one generation to the next.
A student who thinks haploid means half the genes picks this. Every haploid gamete carries a full set of genes; the offspring inherits two complete sets, one from each parent.
A student who thinks mitosis doubles the chromosome number picks this. Mitosis maintains the number; it is fertilization that would double it, and meiosis compensates for fertilization.

mcqs.q: A child has Down syndrome. Both parents have 46 chromosomes in each of their body cells. Which statement about the origin of the condition in this child is correct?
options: A mutation in the zygote altered the base sequence of one gene on chromosome 21, so the child carries a faulty allele of that gene.
One parent produced a gamete with 24 chromosomes because chromosome 21 failed to separate in meiosis, so the zygote had 47 chromosomes.
The extra chromosome 21 was produced at fertilization, when the nuclei of a normal sperm and a normal egg fused and their chromosomes combined.
One parent's meiosis gave a gamete two copies of chromosome 21, and every other gamete from that division had the normal number of 23.
mcqs.specStatementText: Non-disjunction and Down syndrome
mcqs.explain: Non-disjunction is an error of meiosis: the two chromosomes 21, or their chromatids, fail to separate and both go into one gamete, which has 24 chromosomes. Fertilization by a normal gamete with 23 gives a zygote with three copies of chromosome 21 and 47 chromosomes in total.
rationales: A student who thinks every genetic condition is a gene mutation picks this. The genes on chromosome 21 are normal; the condition arises because a whole extra copy of the chromosome is present in every cell.

Non-disjunction is an error of meiosis: the two chromosomes 21, or their chromatids, fail to separate and both go into one gamete, which has 24 chromosomes. Fertilization by a normal gamete with 23 gives a zygote with three copies of chromosome 21 and 47 chromosomes in total.

A student who places the error at the moment the zygote forms picks this. Fusion of two normal gametes gives 46 chromosomes; the extra copy was already present in one gamete because of non-disjunction in meiosis.

A student who has only seen the trisomic outcome drawn picks this. When both copies go to one pole, the other pole receives none, so another gamete from the same division lacks chromosome 21 altogether.

mcqs.q: Which statement about crossing over is correct?
options: Sister chromatids of one chromosome exchange lengths of DNA, so that the two chromatids come to differ from each other.
The exchange of DNA alters the base sequence at the exchanged region, creating new alleles of the genes found there.
The exchange between chromatids decides which chromosome of each pair moves to each pole of the cell in anaphase I.
Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange lengths of DNA, producing new combinations of alleles.
mcqs.specStatementText: Meiosis makes variation: random orientation and crossing over
mcqs.explain: Crossing over occurs in prophase I, while homologous chromosomes are paired as a bivalent. Non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding lengths of DNA, so each chromatid carries a new combination of the alleles present on the two homologues.
rationales: A student who remembers 'chromatids exchange segments' without 'non-sister' picks this. Sister chromatids are identical, so exchanging DNA between them could produce no new combination.
A student who confuses new combinations with new alleles picks this. Crossing over exchanges existing alleles between homologues; new alleles arise only by mutation.
A student who merges crossing over with random orientation picks this. Which homologue goes to which pole is decided by the random orientation of the bivalent at metaphase I, a separate process.

Crossing over occurs in prophase I, while homologous chromosomes are paired as a bivalent. Non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding lengths of DNA, so each chromatid carries a new combination of the alleles present on the two homologues.

mcqs.q: A species has a diploid number of 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes can random orientation of bivalents produce in its gametes?
options: 16, because each of the 4 bivalents can be oriented in 2 ways, independently of the others
8, because each of the 4 bivalents contributes 2 possible orientations to the total
256, because each of the 8 chromosomes can be oriented in 2 ways, independently of the others
4, because a gamete receives one chromosome from each of the 4 bivalents, giving 4 combinations
mcqs.specStatementText: Meiosis makes variation: random orientation and crossing over
mcqs.explain: There are 4 bivalents (2n = 8, so n = 4). Each can be oriented with its maternal or its paternal chromosome facing a given pole, and the orientations are independent, so the number of combinations is 2⁴ = 16.
rationales: There are 4 bivalents (2n = 8, so n = 4). Each can be oriented with its maternal or its paternal chromosome facing a given pole, and the orientations are independent, so the number of combinations is 2⁴ = 16.
A student who adds the possibilities (2 + 2 + 2 + 2) or multiplies 2 × 4 picks this. Independent orientations multiply, giving 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.
A student who uses the diploid number instead of the number of bivalents picks this. Chromosomes orient as pairs, so the exponent is the number of bivalents, 4, not 8: 2⁴, not 2⁸.
A student who counts the bivalents instead of multiplying their orientations picks this. Each of the 4 bivalents has 2 orientations, and independent orientations multiply: 2⁴ = 16.

mcqs.q: Which pair of examples correctly matches cell proliferation to its role?
options: Cells throughout the stem and leaves of a plant dividing: growth; cells in an early-stage animal embryo dividing: repair of damage to the embryo.
Cells in the meristems of a plant dividing: growth; cells beneath the surface of the skin dividing: routine replacement of cells shed from the surface.
Cells at the surface of the skin dividing to replace themselves as they wear away: cell replacement; cells in the meristems of a plant dividing: growth.
Cells at the edge of a skin wound enlarging to fill the gap: wound healing; cells in an early-stage animal embryo dividing: growth.
mcqs.specStatementText: Proliferation for growth, replacement and repair
mcqs.explain: Proliferation for growth in plants is confined to meristems. In skin, cells lost from the surface are continually replaced by proliferation of cells beneath it, an example of routine cell replacement.
rationales: A student who models plant growth on an animal embryo picks this. Mature stem and leaf cells do not normally divide; proliferation for growth happens in meristems, and in an early embryo it is for growth, not repair.

Proliferation for growth in plants is confined to meristems. In skin, cells lost from the surface are continually replaced by proliferation of cells beneath it, an example of routine cell replacement.

A student who assumes replacement happens where loss occurs picks this. The cells shed from the skin surface are not the ones that divide; routine replacement depends on proliferation of cells beneath the surface, which move outwards to replace those lost.

A student who pictures wound closure as stretching picks this. Healing of a skin wound is an example of proliferation: cells at the wound edge divide repeatedly to produce the new cells that fill the gap.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly gives the sequence of phases in the cell cycle?
options: Interphase, made up of G1 and G2, is followed by S, in which the DNA is replicated, and then by mitosis and cytokinesis.
Interphase, a resting period in which the cell is inactive, is followed by mitosis and then by cytokinesis.
Interphase, made up of G1, S and G2 in that order, is followed by mitosis and then by cytokinesis.
Mitosis, which occupies most of the cycle, is followed by cytokinesis and then by a short interphase of G1, S and G2.
mcqs.specStatementText: The cell cycle: G1, S, G2, mitosis, cytokinesis
mcqs.explain: The cell cycle by which cells proliferate runs G1, S and G2 (the stages of interphase), then mitosis, then cytokinesis; the daughter cells then enter G1 of the next cycle.
rationales: A student who places replication just before mitosis picks this. S phase lies between G1 and G2; by G2 the DNA has already been replicated and the cell is growing and preparing for mitosis.
A student who takes 'interphase' to mean a pause picks this. Interphase is metabolically active: the cell grows, synthesizes proteins and DNA and increases its organelles.
The cell cycle by which cells proliferate runs G1, S and G2 (the stages of interphase), then mitosis, then cytokinesis; the daughter cells then enter G1 of the next cycle.
A student who judges the length of a phase by how much is taught about it picks this. Interphase takes most of the cycle; mitosis is a short part of it, and the sequence is interphase first.

mcqs.q: The mass of DNA per nucleus was measured for many cells from a growing tissue. Most nuclei contained 6.0 pg, a smaller group contained 12.0 pg, and a few contained values between 6.0 and 12.0 pg. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The 12.0 pg nuclei have twice as many chromosomes as the 6.0 pg nuclei, so they belong to cells that have just completed mitosis.
The intermediate values are measurement errors, because the DNA content of a nucleus does not change during the inactivity of interphase.
The 12.0 pg nuclei are in prophase, when the DNA is replicated to form the chromatids, and every interphase nucleus contains 6.0 pg.
The 6.0 pg nuclei are in G1, the 12.0 pg nuclei have completed S phase and are in G2 or entering mitosis, and the intermediate values are nuclei in S phase.
mcqs.specStatementText: Interphase is busy, not resting
mcqs.explain: DNA is synthesized during S phase of interphase, so a nucleus that has completed replication contains twice the DNA of a G1 nucleus, and a nucleus caught during replication contains an intermediate amount. The chromosome number is the same in all of them.
rationales: A student who equates DNA mass with chromosome number picks this. Replication doubles the DNA without changing the chromosome number, and cells that have just completed mitosis are back at 6.0 pg.

A student who thinks interphase is a resting phase picks this. Interphase includes S phase, in which DNA is actively synthesized, so intermediate values are expected in cells caught during replication.
A student who thinks chromatids are made in prophase picks this. Replication is completed in S phase of interphase, so G2 nuclei already contain 12.0 pg before mitosis begins.

DNA is synthesized during S phase of interphase, so a nucleus that has completed replication contains twice the DNA of a G1 nucleus, and a nucleus caught during replication contains an intermediate amount. The chromosome number is the same in all of them.

mcqs.q: The concentration of one cyclin was measured in cells passing through the cell cycle. It was low in G1, rose through S and G2, peaked as mitosis began and then fell sharply. When a chemical stopped the concentration of this cyclin from rising beyond half its usual peak, the cells remained in G2. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: A threshold concentration of this cyclin must be reached to pass the checkpoint that allows the cell to enter mitosis.
This cyclin acts as a brake on the cycle, so the cells could not enter mitosis because its concentration had failed to fall.
The concentration of a cyclin should rise continuously through the whole cycle, so the sharp fall shows that these cells had died.
Once a cyclin reaches its peak it stays at that level, so the sharp fall shows that the cells had left the cycle.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cyclins let the cell pass checkpoints
mcqs.explain: The cyclin rises towards mitosis, and cells that cannot accumulate enough of it are held in G2. This is what is expected if a threshold level of a specific cyclin is required to pass the checkpoint into mitosis.
rationales: The cyclin rises towards mitosis, and cells that cannot accumulate enough of it are held in G2. This is what is expected if a threshold level of a specific cyclin is required to pass the checkpoint into mitosis.

A student who thinks cyclins hold the cell back picks this. The cyclin rises before mitosis and the cells that could not raise it enough were the ones held back, so it is a signal to proceed, not a brake.
A student who pictures one cyclin rising steadily picks this. Cyclin concentrations rise and fall during the cycle; the fall after the peak is normal, not a sign of death.
A student who treats a checkpoint as a switch thrown once picks this. A cyclin's concentration falls again after its checkpoint has been passed; the fall is part of the normal cycle.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the control of the cell cycle by cyclins is correct?
options: A single cyclin increases steadily in concentration throughout the cycle, and its level at any moment tells the cell which phase it is in.
The concentrations of different cyclins rise and fall at different points in the cycle, and a threshold level of a specific cyclin is needed to pass each checkpoint.
Cyclins hold the cell at each checkpoint, and the cell passes through only when the concentration of the relevant cyclin falls below a threshold.
Once the concentration of a cyclin has risen above the threshold for a checkpoint, it stays at that high level for the rest of the cycle.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cyclins let the cell pass checkpoints
mcqs.explain: Cyclins are a group of proteins whose concentrations increase and decrease during the cycle. Each checkpoint is passed only when the concentration of a particular cyclin has reached a threshold level.
rationales: A student who remembers one rising line picks this. There are several cyclins, and each rises to a peak and then falls at its own point in the cycle.

Cyclins are a group of proteins whose concentrations increase and decrease during the cycle. Each checkpoint is passed only when the concentration of a particular cyclin has reached a threshold level.
A student who reads 'control' as 'stop' picks this. A rise in cyclin concentration above the threshold is what allows the checkpoint to be passed.
A student who pictures a one-way switch picks this. After the checkpoint is passed the cyclin's concentration decreases again, which is why the cycle can repeat.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes how mutations in genes that control the cell cycle lead to uncontrolled cell division?
options: Mutations make both proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes over-active, so both kinds of gene then stimulate division more strongly.
An oncogene is a gene that a healthy cell does not possess, so uncontrolled division can begin only when one is introduced from outside.
A mutation can turn a proto-oncogene into an oncogene that drives division, or stop a tumour suppressor gene restraining division.
Mutations in cell-cycle genes occur in gametes, so uncontrolled division appears only in the offspring that inherit the mutated gene.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mutations in cell-cycle genes drive uncontrolled division
mcqs.explain: Proto-oncogenes are normal genes whose products promote the cell cycle; a mutation can make one an oncogene with an over-active product. Tumour suppressor genes restrain the cycle; mutations that disable them remove that restraint. Either change results in uncontrolled division.
rationales: A student who treats all cancer-related mutations alike picks this. A tumour suppressor mutation is a loss of function: the product that would halt division no longer works.
A student who reads 'oncogene' as a foreign cancer gene picks this. Every cell has proto-oncogenes; a mutation in one of the cell's own genes converts it into an oncogene.

Proto-oncogenes are normal genes whose products promote the cell cycle; a mutation can make one an oncogene with an over-active product. Tumour suppressor genes restrain the cycle; mutations that disable them remove that restraint. Either change results in uncontrolled division.
A student who assumes all mutations are inherited picks this. Most such mutations arise in somatic cells and cause a tumour in the individual in which they occur; they are not passed on.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes between types of tumour?
options: A benign tumour is a harmless overgrowth of normal tissue, not the result of uncontrolled division, so it is not a true tumour.
A secondary tumour is a second tumour that arises independently in a different tissue, from a different set of mutations.
A malignant tumour is one that grows faster and reaches a larger size than a benign tumour; size and rate of growth define which is which.
A malignant tumour invades neighbouring tissue and can spread to form secondary tumours; a benign tumour does neither and does not cause cancer.
mcqs.specStatementText: Benign versus malignant, and measuring the mitotic index
mcqs.explain: Malignant tumours invade neighbouring tissue and have the capacity for metastasis, forming secondary tumours; they cause cancer. Benign tumours stay in one place, do not invade or spread and do not cause cancer.
rationales: A student who takes 'benign' to mean 'normal' picks this. A benign tumour is formed by uncontrolled division; it is benign because its cells do not invade or spread, not because they are normal.
A student who hears 'secondary' as 'another one' picks this. A secondary tumour is formed by cells that spread from the primary tumour by metastasis; it is not an independent tumour.
A student who equates cancer with speed of growth picks this. Tumours of both kinds vary in growth rate; malignancy is defined by invasion and the capacity for metastasis.

Malignant tumours invade neighbouring tissue and have the capacity for metastasis, forming secondary tumours; they cause cancer. Benign tumours stay in one place, do not invade or spread and do not cause cancer.

mcqs.q: A student examined 240 cells in a micrograph of a growing tissue. 204 cells had an intact nucleus with no visible chromosomes, and the remaining 36 cells had condensed chromosomes visible. What is the mitotic index of the sample?
mcqs.specStatementText: Benign versus malignant, and measuring the mitotic index
mcqs.explain: Cells with condensed chromosomes are in mitosis; those with an intact nucleus and no visible chromosomes are in interphase. Mitotic index = number of cells in mitosis ÷ total number of cells observed = 36 ÷ 240 = 0.15 (15%).
rationales: Cells with condensed chromosomes are in mitosis; those with an intact nucleus and no visible chromosomes are in interphase. Mitotic index = number of cells in mitosis ÷ total number of cells observed = 36 ÷ 240 = 0.15 (15%).
A student who divides the dividing cells by the non-dividing cells picks this: 36 ÷ 204 = 0.18. The denominator of the mitotic index is the total number of cells, 240.

A student who expects most cells to be in mitosis assumes the larger group must be the dividing one and calculates 204 ÷ 240. An intact nucleus with no visible chromosomes is the appearance of interphase; only the 36 cells with condensed chromosomes are in mitosis.

A student who counts a cell with an intact nucleus as being in prophase treats all 240 cells as dividing, giving 240 ÷ 240. Interphase is not a phase of mitosis, so the 204 cells with an intact nucleus are excluded.

mcqs.q: The mitotic index was determined for three samples: cells from a root-tip meristem, 0.12; cells from a tumour removed from a patient, 0.10; cells from a mature leaf, 0.00. A student concluded that the tumour must be benign because its mitotic index is lower than that of a healthy meristem. Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?
options: It is not justified: a mitotic index as high as 0.12 shows that the meristem itself is cancerous, so it cannot serve as a healthy tissue for comparison.
It is not justified: the mitotic index measures how many cells are dividing, but malignancy depends on the capacity to invade tissue and metastasize.
It is justified: malignant tumours are defined by dividing faster than normal tissue, so a tumour dividing more slowly than a meristem is benign.
It is not justified: benign tumours have a mitotic index of zero because their cells have stopped dividing, so this tumour must be malignant.
mcqs.specStatementText: Benign versus malignant, and measuring the mitotic index
mcqs.explain: A mitotic index shows the rate of proliferation. Benign and malignant tumours both divide uncontrollably and vary in rate; malignancy is defined by invasion of neighbouring tissue and metastasis, which a count of dividing cells cannot reveal.
rationales: A student who reads all rapid division as cancer picks this. A meristem is a normal tissue that proliferates for growth; a high mitotic index there is expected and is not evidence of a tumour.

A mitotic index shows the rate of proliferation. Benign and malignant tumours both divide uncontrollably and vary in rate; malignancy is defined by invasion of neighbouring tissue and metastasis, which a count of dividing cells cannot reveal.
A student who defines malignancy by growth rate picks this. Rates of division vary among tumours of both kinds; the defining feature of a malignant tumour is invasion and the capacity for metastasis.

A student who thinks 'benign' means the cells are not dividing picks this. A benign tumour is itself the product of uncontrolled division and has a mitotic index well above zero; the index cannot settle the question either way.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic D2.1 Cell and nuclear division

specStatements.text: New cells only come from cells dividing
Cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm, differently in animals and plants
Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not always
Mitosis keeps the genome; meiosis halves it and adds variety
DNA is replicated once before either division
Chromosomes condense and are moved by microtubules in both divisions
Reading the phase from a diagram or micrograph
Meiosis: two divisions, one diploid nucleus to four haploid
Meiosis makes variation: random orientation and crossing over
Proliferation for growth, replacement and repair
The cell cycle: G1, S, G2, mitosis, cytokinesis
Cyclins let the cell pass checkpoints
Mutations in cell-cycle genes drive uncontrolled division
Benign versus malignant, and measuring the mitotic index

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Skin is used only as the guidance requires: as an example of proliferation for routine replacement of cells lost from the surface and for wound healing. No layer of the skin is named (no epidermis, dermis, stratum basale or basal layer), and no cell type, structure or process specific to skin beyond 'cells beneath the surface divide and the new cells replace those shed' is mentioned.

No cyclin is named (no cyclin A, B, D or E), no cyclin-dependent kinase is mentioned, and no checkpoint is linked to a named cyclin. The objects test only that different cyclins rise and fall at different points in the cycle, that a threshold concentration of a specific cyclin is required to pass a checkpoint, and that the concentration falls again afterwards; the data item describes 'one cyclin' without naming it.
